#1874. Chelsea: Mykhailo Mudryk points finger for drugs ban as Tottenham loan star prepares for comeback

Your weekly briefing on Chelsea, featuring team news and expert analysis from Dom Smith

Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed the Ukrainian football association for his doping ban.

The Chelsea winger, currently on loan at Tottenham, sat out the entirety of the 2025-26 season due to a positive drugs test for meldonium, a banned substance, back in October 2024.

The substance is believed to enhance stamina and respiratory capacity.

The forward was allowed to play once more in the summer, when his four-year ban, that he appealed through the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), was lifted.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso pushed for the winger to go out on loan to earn regular game time, and he reunited with his former boss at Shakhtar Donetsk, Roberto De Zerbi, at Spurs.

Now, Mudryk has pointed the finger at the Ukrainian FA for the ‘adverse finding’ in his out-of-competition sample that was supplied two years ago.

"It was a bolt from the blue,” he said of his positive drugs test on Ukrainian podcast ‘Guest of Gordon’.

“I couldn’t believe it was true. It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on failing. It hit me very hard, mentally.”

The 25-year-old claims that he had never heard of meldonium, insisting that there was “no security” on international duty.

“It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe,” he explained. “It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England.”

Asked how it had got into his system, he replied: "The Ukrainian national team has absolutely no security system. At clubs, when you travel to an away game, there are always people responsible for what happens on the hotel floors and in the team.

“There are people who keep an eye on it. In the Ukrainian national team we have a nutritionist who hands us pills every couple of days before games.

“He brings us a little cup. Everyone has to take the pills that are in that cup.”

The winger, who moved to Stamford Bridge in 2023 for an initial £62million - that could rise to £89m - was asked point-blank if he blamed his national setup.

He is hoped to be back this weekend for Spurs’ home game against Ipswich.

#1873. CorSport: Fontanella-Khan up and running within Milan’s management – his background and role

James Fontanella-Khan is up and running with his new position at AC Milan, following an interesting background which includes the former Rossoneri man Alberto Gilardino.

It was in the middle of September that various outlets reported that Fontanella-Khan was joining Milan’s management as the new Chief Corporate Affairs Officer. Two months have passed since and the 43-year-old is now up and running with his new gig.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

He has been spotted among the top brass in the stands of San Siro during the most recent games and he was also present at the dinner Gerry Cardinale hosted before the derby. In other words, he’s not exactly working remotely, instead expected to spend most of his time in Milan.

Today’s edition of Corriere dello Sport (via MilanNews) has taken a closer look at Fontanella-Khan, who has various valuable experiences to rely on in his new gig. Most recently, he was the US Financial Editor for the Financial Times, even moderating some conferences that Cardinale spoke at.

Before making waves in the US, however, he actually grew up in Italy and even played football himself. He was a goalkeeper in Piacenza’s youth team, reaching the Primavera of the club, and he was even a teammate of Alberto Gilardino (the former Milan striker) at one point.

After deciding that football wasn’t his path in life, he left Italy to start an internship for the Financial Times in London. He worked his way up and remained at the newspaper for over 20 years before accepting the Milan gig.

As for his role with Milan, according to Corriere dello Sport, he could be described as a General Manager. He handles communications, politics (he will be present at the League assemblies), and represents the club at various events.

Part of his goal is to connect the US mentality of the Rossoneri ownership with the Italian identity of the club, partly relying on his background as a footballer and Milan fan.

#1870. Aston Villa linked with cut-price January move for Ruben Loftus-Cheek

Aston Villa has emerged as a possible destination for Ruben Loftus-Cheek, with AC Milan reportedly prepared to accept between €4 million and €5 million for the midfielder in January.

Calciomercato’s Daniele Longo reports that Milan would consider an early departure before the Englishman’s contract expires in the summer of 2027. A winter sale would bring in a fee and remove his salary from the wage bill.

Villa is identified as a destination that could appeal to Loftus-Cheek, while Besiktas could revive its own interest. There is no reported offer from Unai Emery’s club at this stage.

The player’s preference could complicate Milan’s plans. Longo suggests that Loftus-Cheek and his representatives may favor waiting until the summer, when a free transfer would give him greater freedom to choose his next club and negotiate personal terms.

The former Chelsea midfielder has made seven Serie A appearances this season, according to Sport Witness. He is currently recovering from injury, with Calciomercato reporting that a return to group training is expected around the end of November or early December.

Jurgen Kloppai??i??s countrymen are well versed with the appeal of quick fixes. They once allowed one of historyai??i??s most hated figures to rise to power. In the summer windows, one can look at options beyond these two. #1868. Pedro Porro to Barcelona: Could Spain international move to Camp Nou in January?

By Matt Law | 17 Nov 2026 08:23, Last updated: 17 Nov 2026 08:25

Barcelona will reportedly not make a move for Tottenham Hotspur defender Pedro Porro during the January transfer window, but a switch to Camp Nou next summer is a possibility.

Porro, 27, has had his issues at Tottenham, but the right-back was outstanding for Spain at the 2026 World Cup and is an important player for the national side.

There has recently been speculation surrounding Porro's future, with Barcelona planning to be active during the January market due to their defensive issues.

Barcelona had allegedly been open to the idea of signing Porro in the winter market, providing that a suitable deal could be agreed with Tottenham.

According to journalist Matteo Moretto, the La Liga champions will not be moving for Porro when the January window opens for business.

However, a future switch to Camp Nou has not been ruled out, with Barcelona potentially reigniting their interest during next summer's transfer window.

Porro said at the end of last month that he wants to return to La Liga before the end of his career.

"Obviously, I’d love to return to Spain someday. It’s my country, and I like the league," he told El Larguero.

"Right now, it would be very unfair to talk about anything other than my club because I’m under contract, but obviously, I’d love to go back to Spain; it’s a big dream of mine."

Porro also recently said that he was 'flattered' to be of interest to Barcelona.

"Yes, of course it's flattering," he said in an interview with SPORT.

"When one of the best clubs in the world is interested in you, or at least that's what they say, it's always a good thing, because it probably means I'm doing my job well. I have to keep going in the same direction."

Porro has previously played in La Liga for Girona and Real Valladolid, but he has not operated in Spain since 2020.

The right-back joined Tottenham from Sporting Lisbon in January 2023, and he has represented his North London club on 159 occasions, scoring 13 goals and registering 26 assists in the process.

#1867. Liverpool vs Arsenal Preview: Team News, Tactics, Lineups and Prediction

Home » Home 2 » Liverpool vs Arsenal Preview: Team News, Tactics, Lineups and Prediction

Table-toppers Arsenal travel to Anfield tonight with their first Premier League trophy since the ‘invincibles’ season of 2004 in sight. The Gunners top the table and with stuttering performances from Manchester City and a Leicester City whose fairytale run seems at an end, and are in pole position to finish the current campaign as champions.

While Jurgen Klopp’s men are still finding their way inconsistently since his appointment, Arsenal are in top form with five victories out of their last six matches. In comparison, Liverpool have been as easy to predict as a magic 8 ball, with impressive wins over Leicester City and Manchester City, but accompanied with horrific losses against Watford and West Ham. With fourth place still within grasp and with an impressive record against the table topping teams this season, Liverpool would look to give their long suffering fans some cheer with which to greet this New Year.

The Reds desperately need a victory to steady the ship as their erratic and wayward form sees them enter 2016 still outside the top 4 and distant from any title challenge.

With a host of injuries to his main XI, Jurgen Klopp could be forgiven for dipping into the transfer market so early. The Reds have captured QPR right-back Steven Caulker along with Marko Grujic in the January transfer window.

With Grujic returning to his former club Red Star Belgrade on loan, Steven Caulker is likely to be given a run out as a substitute with the current spate of Liverpool injuries.

Ings, Sturridge, Lovren, Coutinho, Origi and Flanagan are amongst the Liverpool afflicted and will take no part in the match ahead. With Lovren out, Kolo Toure and Mamadou Sakho look likely to be Klopp’s first choice central defending partnership.

Alberto Moreno and Nathaniel Clyne should start as full-backs for the Liverpool side and will be crucial in any attempt to penetrate the Gunner’s defences. Emre Can and Lucas should marshal the midfield, while James Milner, Firmino and Adam Lallana look to give Petr Cech some concerns about his goal. Leading the line should be Christian Benteke, who’s lack of form doesn’t threaten this match as manager Klopp has few options in his position.

Probable Starting XI (4-5-1): Mignolet; Clyne, Sakho, Toure, Moreno; Lucas, Can, Firmino, Lallana, Milner, Benteke.

Arsenal must show that they have the one quality required of all champions : Consistency. The task is hereby straightforward for Wenger’s men. Win, keep winning, regardless of your manner and the title is yours.

With half the season concluded, Arsene Wenger must be wishing that he received a Christmas gift from the Arsenal medical team. Injuries have decimated his midfield with Wilshire, Cazorla, Rosiscky, Coquelin and Sanchez out of the game.

There is some good news with Mesul Ozil having managed to partake in some leisure instead of participating in the FA cup victory over Sunderland. Keeping the nimble playmaker fit would be key to Arsenal aspirations, both in this match and for the remainder of the season.

With both Petr Mertersacker and Gabriel available, it would be interesting to see whom Arsene Wenger picks out for his starting XI. Koscielny, Bellerin and Monreal have nailed down their place in the defence and the inclusion of the slower Mertersacker or the inconsistent Gabriel may have a defining moment in the game.

With Arsenal’s midfield woes, it should fall to Flamini to screen the defence with Ramsey alongside him. Walcott, Ozil and Joel Campbell should be the main thrusts of Arsenal’s attacking play with Giroud as the elegant, decisive focus.

Probable Starting XI (4-5-1): Cech; Bellerin, Gabriel, Koscielny, Monreal; Flamini, Ramsey, Ozil, Walcott, Campbell; Girourd.

With previous encounters between these teams resulting in high scoring draws, we favour a repeat of last year’s epic 2-2 result for the same fixture. Martin Skrtel’s 97th minute header in front of the Kop capped a memorable game which also had Fabio Borini sent off and we expect similar fireworks at Anfield tomorrow.

#1866. Gila discusses his mental health journey, perfectionism and current state: “Changed my perspective”

In the latest episode of AC Milan’s The Chamber series, Mario Gila was the guest and spoke about the positive mental health journey that he’s currently on.

It was last month that Milan unveiled their new series, called The Chamber, which focuses on the mental health of the players at the club. Luka Modric was the first guest, a perfect start in many ways, and the second episode has now been published with Mario Gila as the guest.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The concept, in case you’re not familiar, is that the players are placed in a ‘Chamber’ with no outside noise for a few minutes. Then, they are interviewed by the host Luca Casadei, who focuses on the mental state of the players.

As said, Gila was the guest in the most recent edition and he has a lot to say, having been on a mental health journey in the last few years. Indeed, after hitting ‘rock-bottom’ at Lazio, he found a way through and is now very happy.

How are you feeling right now? [after being in the chamber, editor’s note]

I feel very peaceful, I feel really good here. I think experiences like this are also closely linked to how a person feels and where they are emotionally at that moment. And I think it amplifies everything… a little. I wanted to experience it to the fullest when they told me about it.

I think when there are no outside influences clouding your mind that’s when you connect most with yourself. That’s why I closed my eyes. I wanted to feel as deeply as possible what was inside me and how my mind works in moments like this.”

What did you feel during this experience?

Well, I really enjoyed it because I felt so peaceful. I felt completely at ease, and it was an experience I’ve rarely had before. I’m someone who likes to meditate, to reconnect with myself, and I’m interested in spirituality, it’s something I genuinely enjoy.

“And I felt so much peace, so much peace because with everything so quiet, such complete silence and being in touch with myself, it really is an experience I’m not sure I’ll ever forget. I really liked it.”

Speaking about yourself, are there moments when you’re alone, away from the public eye, away from everyone expecting something of you, when you take some time just for yourself? I’d like to know what you feel, who you are emotionally in those moments.

It doesn’t happen to me often because, whether you like it or not, footballers tend to have very active minds. It’s a profession that takes a huge mental toll.

“But I try, for example, during holidays or whenever we get some time off, to find situations where I feel, well, maybe not exactly like in that chamber, but where I can connect with myself, where I can rediscover that Mario who sometimes gets a little lost because of the job he does.

“And in those moments, well, I feel at peace, I feel that connection with myself, I feel like a person. Because in our profession, whether we like it or not, we lose touch with ourselves a little. And that’s what I’m trying to achieve when I’m alone with myself.”

You told me that because of the job you do, you’re always very focused. I wanted to talk about control because I’ve heard you say you need to have everything under control.

Yes, I think that, given the way I see the profession and the position we footballers are in, I think it may not seem like it, but you have a lot of things to manage. How you behave off the pitch, you’re a footballer 24 hours a day, your diet, physical preparation, training sessions, the physio.

And it’s like… I have to keep everything perfectly under control so that at the weekend or in a midweek match I’m at my best.  So the profession itself pushes you to keep everything under control and if you’re also someone who likes that and believes things should be that way, you take it even further.

“And in those situations, I feel comfortable when everything’s under control.”

Is that just at work, or does it apply everywhere, with your family, your friends, always needing to have everything under control?

I’ve been like that with my family too, with my teammates, with my friends, but I see my personal life differently now. I didn’t before. Because perfection is exhausting.  In the end, so many expectations… Striving for perfection wears you out.

“I think that, to a certain extent, it’s boring. You don’t get to see the real person, their authentic self. So that’s how I’ve been for much of my life. I’m young, but I’ve been like that. Now I’m beginning to understand better that everyone is different, that every moment is different, and to appreciate that more, that authenticity.

Did you used to feel weak when you weren’t in control? Vulnerable?

Now, though, you’ve realised it’s a strength?

“Yes, yes, yes. I understand that people and situations aren’t always as we want or expect them to be. And I think it’s somewhat connected to ego, but now we’re getting into some pretty deep territory. But…I like it! I think so, yes, I used to be like that. I used to be. I’m less like that now, and I appreciate difficult moments more because there’s also a lot of good to be found in those moments.

“I mean, we can’t control everything, we can’t expect everything to be perfect because perfection doesn’t teach you anything. I don’t think there’s anything particularly positive about it.

“In the end, we grow a lot through… or we become stronger during difficult times than during good ones. So I’ve largely let go of that kind of perfectionism. And those incredibly high expectations, I don’t like them anymore.”

But is there a positive side to perfectionism for you? Do you think you became the player you are thanks to your perfectionism?

“Yes. This is a struggle I have with myself, for example. In this profession, I believe that perfectionism and ego are two things that drive us to succeed at work, in our professional lives. Ego drives you to be better than, say, the opponent you’re playing against.

“Perfectionism makes you work harder, train better, take better care of yourself and I think that helps you develop a lot professionally. But there has to be a balance. It can’t all be about perfectionism because it makes you incredibly demanding of yourself and when you go through difficult times, you won’t know how to deal with them.

When you make a mistake, are you very demanding and hard on yourself? I mean, how do you treat yourself when something doesn’t go the way you wanted?

“In the past, for example… I’ve changed a great deal. I went through a really difficult time early in my career here in Italy and hit rock bottom, but with outside help, psychological support, I got through it.

“That’s why I keep saying ‘before’. Back then, I was very hard on myself. I didn’t allow myself to fail. If I did, I was extremely negative towards myself, I couldn’t accept that I might fail or make mistakes.

“Now I handle it much better. Now I feel that making mistakes is part of the job, it’s something that helps you improve, something that helps you grow. So I deal with it much more calmly, I process it much better internally.

“I think you still need to hold yourself to high standards and you also need to know how to find a solution to that mistake, whether in your career or in your personal life, but with much more calm and more kindness towards myself.”

This interview is also meant to share some values with others, right? In those moments, what exactly do you tell yourself to be kinder to yourself?

“Well… What a good question! In moments when I’ve gone through difficult situations, perhaps, after that period I was telling you about, I’m aware that everyone can make mistakes. I know that making mistakes is part of the job and it’s what helps me grow.

“So I changed my perspective. I used to see it very negatively, now I find the positive in the negative. So I understand that if I focus on something positive or look at it from a positive perspective, everything surrounding the mistake changes.

“All that noise stops being noise and turns into a sense of calm. It’s normal to make a mistake and be demanding of yourself, to want to avoid making that mistake again, but it might still happen.

“So at that moment, I believe that being kind to yourself and recognising that it’s something that can happen and that you can use it to improve, is, I think, the way forward to avoid falling into negativity. But instead maintain that positivity and balance that can help you feel at peace, as I was saying in there, like the experience I had in there earlier.”

Regarding that difficult period you went through, which helped you grow and taught you so many things, you mentioned therapy. Could you tell me, not so much what happened, but what your experience with therapy was like? I mean, what did it give you at first?

“I sought help from a psychologist because I was going through a very difficult time and couldn’t find a way to move forward. We’re expected to deal with situations… that I find mentally overwhelming, at just 21 years old, when you have no professional experience, because in the end, everything comes at you so fast.

“So I went to a psychologist, and completely changed my perspective. I mean, I started seeing everything negative that happened to me as a step forward, thinking: this is something that will help you improve, something you needed to go through.

“Everything changed when I changed my perspective. I used to be very hard on myself, very hard, I demanded so much of myself. Now I’m someone who feels much more at ease.

“We can all fail, make mistakes, go through difficult situations, So the way I treat myself, the way I respond to myself, the way I talk to myself, I think it plays a crucial role in maintaining a consistently positive mindset.”

Today, with the maturity and mindset you’ve developed, how do you handle pressure? Those moments when expectations are high, when your heart starts beating faster, how do you deal with those moments?

“It depends. Because speaking for myself, I see pressure as something that helps give me that extra push to… I mean, I’m someone who believes that footballers naturally feel pressure or feel a little nervous before a match, even the day before, depending on the match, some matches are more important than others, but you still feel that pressure.

“I think accepting that pressure is positive because it helps prepare you, but I haven’t had situations where pressure has paralysed me, because I experienced that in the past.

“In the past, I’ve felt that kind of pressure, and pressure that paralyses you is very negative because it’s very different from the pressure you feel when you’re in a good place mentally, which helps you prepare.

“It’s a kind of pressure, the pressure I used to feel, that completely paralyses you, it’s a pressure that makes your heart race, that makes you afraid, so they’re two different kinds of pressure. I’ve experienced both.

“The first is difficult to handle because it’s anxiety, the expectation of performing well, it’s the feeling that so many people are watching you, you have to perform well, you have to play well, and that gets into your head, and I don’t think it’s very positive.

“The other, on the other hand, helps you prepare, you feel a little nervous, you get that slight feeling of getting yourself ready, but if you manage to channel it properly, it becomes something that prepares you, a natural response to having something important to face.”

Listening to you speak and watching you play, I see someone who’s very composed. That confidence you have in yourself, have you always had it? Where does it come from?

“I’m someone who has always given the impression of being very confident. I mean, I’ve always believed I had a lot of confidence in myself, but actually, when things got tough, I didn’t have it because whenever I went through a difficult time, I doubted myself a lot.

“I think you develop that through psychological work, but also by feeling confident in your work. Those things go hand in hand. I mean, it’s not all down to the psychologist and nothing to do with my career.

“No. I mean, everything has gone hand in hand. When I started going through this process, things also started going really well for me in football, which helped along the way. So I’ve managed to develop confidence in both areas, which has made me the person I am today, someone who I believe really does have a lot of confidence in himself, because I genuinely feel it.

“It’s something I’ve worked on a lot, learning to believe in yourself, not because of what other people say or the value others place on you, but because of the value you give yourself. And that’s where I’ve found my stability, my peace and my confidence in that environment.

You’ve played alongside some incredible players. How did you manage… I mean, did you use the comparison with their talent as a way to grow rather than feeling envious, as something positive to help you improve?

“Yes. The thing is, this is very closely connected to confidence. You know? When you believe in yourself and have that confidence, you learn to appreciate what you can learn from others. If you’re perhaps someone who doesn’t have much confidence in yourself, you might feel envious of others.

“And then you fail to recognise the lesson that the other person is teaching you, even when you can learn just by watching them. So I began to understand that when I started reaching a place of emotional wellbeing, where I was more focused on the present.

“Before, because I had less confidence in myself, I compared myself to others more. Maybe I didn’t appreciate what someone else was doing or perhaps I couldn’t fully appreciate what they were trying to teach me.

“Once you manage to build a solid sense of confidence and truly believe in yourself, you see what others can teach you in a positive light. And you see it as an opportunity to grow, you look at it from a different perspective.

“So it’s not just about what people might be teaching you directly. I’ve learned from many players just by watching, just by paying attention. But sometimes I’ve learned from negative things too. I mean, not just from positive things. I understand that learning isn’t just about someone saying: ‘Listen, you need to do this, and I think you should do it this way’.

“No, it’s also about how they behave. For example, right now we have Luka Modric in the team. And I pay a lot of attention to him, to how he behaves, to the humility he shows, to how he handles different situations.

“And that’s something you understand when you’re comfortable with yourself. If you’re not comfortable with yourself, I don’t think you’ll be able to understand that. I mean, you won’t see the other person as a positive example. You’ll see them in a negative light.

And when you’re experiencing a great moment, are you able to recognise it? To feel proud of yourself? To enjoy that moment of happiness? To stop and appreciate it?

“That’s something I struggle with, for example. It’s something I find difficult because I’m aware of it, but I think it’s something that people generally struggle with because we tend to notice the negative things more or give more importance to difficult moments than to the positive ones.

“And I think that’s a mistake everyone makes, I don’t know why. But I’m trying to work on it, I’m aware of it. But I have to tell you that if we were to compare how much I enjoy the good moments with how much I suffer during the bad ones, no.

“I suffer more during the bad moments than I enjoy the good ones. And unfortunately, that’s something I still haven’t learned how to manage or how to truly enjoy those positive moments because we’re also here to enjoy the good moments and to experience them fully. But I find that harder than dealing with a difficult moment.”

I really like how much you’ve grown in terms of maturity, everything you’ve come to understand. So I’d like to ask you one last question to reflect on everything. It’s a simple question: How are you?

Not how you are today, but looking at your life, what kind of chapter are you going through right now? Is Mario happy?

Mario is very happy. I mean, this whole conversation we’ve had has a lot to do with the positive place I’m in right now. If I were going through a difficult time, perhaps there are many things I wouldn’t understand the way I do now.

“But I’m in a really good place right now because I’m exactly where I want to be. I’m somewhere I’m appreciated and loved. I became a father a year ago. I have a wife who loves me very much too.

“It’s as though so many things are coming together, things are going well in my career, things are going well with my family. I have friends who I believe are truly valuable people. I also have a family that means so much to me.

“So it’s like everything is going really well right now. So I feel very balanced, I feel very much at peace. I feel like I’m exactly where I want to be. I’m really appreciated. So right now I’m at a very happy point in my life. Very happy.

“If negative things happen, I have a support system I can rely on. I have that support that helps me feel okay. And I think that’s really important because I believe you’ll always experience difficult moments in life. So there’s no way to completely avoid those difficult moments, you can’t, it’s just not possible.

“And life would lose its meaning. But having that safety net and that support system, I think it also allows you to thrive in every other area of your life. So I’m very happy. Right now I feel incredibly happy, very peaceful, very balanced, very happy with myself too, and I’m genuinely very happy we had this conversation because I’m really interested in all these psychological aspects,” he concluded.

#1863. FIFA Slaps Real Madrid, Atletico Madrid With 1-Year Transfer Bans

Home » Home 2 » FIFA Slaps Real Madrid, Atletico Madrid With 1-Year Transfer Bans

The ban will start from the July transfer window this year and finish with the January transfer market in 2017.

Atletico were also fined 900,000 Swiss francs (820,000 euros) and Real 360,000 (330,000 euros).

“The two clubs were found to have violated several provisions concerning the international transfer and first registration of minor players as well as other relevant provisions with regard to the registration and participation of certain players in competitions,” said a FIFA statement.

Barcelona has just ended a one year ban for similar reasons.

Real and Atletico were “issued with a reprimand and given 90 days in which to regularise the situation of all minor players concerned,” FIFA said. They can still sell players during the transfer ban.

FIFA said the alarm was raised over the two clubs by FIFA’s Transfer Matching System and its disciplinary committee completed the inquiry.

Under international football rules, players under 18 cannot be transferred to another country, except in limited circumstances. All transfers need the approval of a special FIFA committee.

“The investigations concerned minor players who were involved and participated in competitions with the clubs over various periods between 2007 and 2014 (Atletico Madrid) and between 2005 and 2014 (Real Madrid),” FIFA said.

The ban follows a similar sanction handed to European champions Barcelona, who were unable to register new players during 2015.

Barca were initially banned in April 2014, but managed to delay the sanction taking affect until the transfer windows in January and the summer 2015 by launching an ultimately unsuccessful appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

By delaying the ban, Barca managed to sign the likes of Luis Suarez and Ivan Rakitic in the summer of 2014 to propel them to a treble of La Liga, Champions League and Copa del Rey.

The news is just the latest institutional embarassment for Real Madrid just over a week after they appointed French legend Zinedine Zidane.

Madrid have sacked two Champions League winning coaches in Carlo Ancelotti and Rafael Benitez in the past seven months, as well as being thrown out of the Copa del Rey for fielding an ineligible player.

The sanction could also be bad news for the likes of Paris Saint-Germain and Manchester United, who had targeted Madrid stars Cristiano Ronaldo and Gareth Bale with Real highly unlikely to dispose of their best players without the chance to sign suitable replacements.

La Liga leaders Atletico Madrid’s usually hectic transfer policy will also be put on hold. However, Diego Simeone’s men look better placed to cope with the ban having invested heavily in young talent over the past year.

Neither Real no Atletico made an immediate comment on whether they would appeal.

#1862. Germany 5-0 Netherlands: Jurgen Klopp sends clear message that spells trouble for Nations League rivals

By Oliver Thomas | 17 Nov 2026 09:46

Jurgen Klopp is in dreamland after witnessing a “truly extraordinary” performance from his Germany side in a statement 5-0 victory over the Netherlands in the UEFA Nations League on Monday.

The four-time world champions began the night sitting third in League A Group 2 and knew that they had to claim maximum points against the Oranje at the summit to secure top spot and qualify for the quarter-finals.

With so much at stake heading into the sixth and final matchday, Die Mannschaft rose to the occasion in prolific fashion, claiming their biggest win against their Dutch neighbours since 1959 when they won 7-0.

Derry Scherhant opened the scoring just before half time with a sensational maiden international goal, setting the tone for a dominant second-half display.

Overwhelmed by Germany’s relentless high press, the Netherlands had no answer as two goals from Florian Wirtz, and strikes from Nico Schlotterbeck and Brajan Gruda, sealed a statement triumph for Klopp’s side.

“What we’ve just witnessed was truly extraordinary,” the former Liverpool manager told reporters post-match. “The game was extraordinary, and incredibly difficult.”

“Against a really good opponent, you have to find a way to win. We had to adapt and make a few adjustments, some fairly significant ones, but we made them. We took away a lot of their strengths, and then we scored some incredible goals. That was unbelievable.

“It was a fantastic football match and a wonderful experience. I wouldn’t have ever dreamed of having the chance to do this in Berlin in front of a sold-out crowd. In the final international game of the year, it’s amazing.”

In addition to progressing to the quarter-finals, the result served as compelling evidence of Germany's renaissance and progress under Klopp, with his arrival fostering renewed optimism around his youthful squad.

Germany failed to win their opening two Nations League matches, but they ended their group campaign with 11 points (W3 D2 L1) and have conceded a competition-low three goals in six games.

"The moment I arrived here, I fell in love with this team at first sight,” said Klopp. “I'm at the beginning of this journey.

“I simply feel that we have a fantastic football team and a very good footballing idea that can work extremely well. If we can get these highly-talented players firing, then we're going to be a very difficult team to play against.

“We scored some incredible goals and, with increasing confidence, put in a great performance in front of a fantastic crowd. It’s been a lot of fun to work with this team, and we feel like we have a very special group of players here.

“But this is still only just the beginning – after six games, we can’t say that we’ve arrived where we want to be yet, as there are still lots of things we can improve on.”

"Everyone who was here today is going home with a smile, and won't be questioning the German national team for the next three or four months. That's a good thing," Klopp added when referring to the negativity that lingered previously around the national team.

Looking ahead to the quarter-final draw on Friday, Klopp added: "The lads can head home now with a smile on their faces as the group winners. We’ll watch the draw later this week and wait and see what sort of crunch match we’ll get, as there are only strong teams left.”

Germany, who have risen to 11th in the FIFA World Rankings, will play their two-legged quarter-final tie in March 2027, with a first-placed finish in League A rewarded with a second leg on home soil.

#1859. Record-breaking Harry Kane belongs in the company of greats that he keeps. There is only one gap in his record now and he remains as central to ending 60 years of hurt than he has ever been, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 16:54 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 20:17 EST, 12 November 2026

Only giants have trodden the path that Harry Kane walked at Wembley on Thursday when he strode out on to the pitch on a bitterly cold winter night, his four young children by his side, and beheld the array of trophies, honours, adulation and respect that awaited him.

It is just 16 days since Kane held his hands to his face, climbed up to the stage at the London Palladium and said 'wow' when Ronaldo 'Il Fenomeno' presented him with the Ballon d'Or trophy that anointed him the best player in the world.

Now, it sat before him on a plinth and Kane broke away from the England line-up and walked forward to hoist it aloft. He showed it to all the corners of the stadium and for a moment, it was framed against the giant tifo bearing his image and the words 'England's Finest' that towered over one end of the ground.

But the Ballon d’Or is old news in the flood of honours that is coming Kane’s way in this golden summer of a great career. Kane had become the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or for a quarter of a century and on Thursday night he was to break the 37-year-old record held by Peter Shilton for the most England caps. He scored the winner, too. Of course, he did.

The occasion of England-Croatia in the Nations League was Kane's 126th appearance in an England shirt and Shilton stepped forward to hand him a small case containing a crest to mark the achievement. Finally, the Prince of Wales showed his appreciation to the England captain by presenting him with a commemorative shirt with 'Kane 126' emblazoned on it.

It was a night to feel the weight of football's history and the ghosts of greatness that people England's heritage. Kane belongs in the company he now keeps. He belongs in the pantheon of the game because he is one of the deadliest strikers in history. He belongs in the pantheon because of the humility he has shown and the dedication he devotes to improvement.

Harry Kane celebrated his record-breaking England appearance with a finely struck penalty

Before kick-off, Kane's history-making was celebrated with a commemorative shirt by the Prince of Wales

England (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; Alexander-Arnold 6 (White 78, 6), Quansah 4, Burn 6, Hall 7; Rice 5 (Garner 78, 5), Anderson 6; Rogers 8, Bellingham 6, Gordon 5 (Ngumoha 78, 5); Kane 7

Croatia (4-2-3-1): Livakovic 5; Smolcic 6 (Marco Pasalic 76 5), Stanisic 6, Vuskovic 6, Gvardiol 5; Misic 5 (Modric 76, 6), Kovacic 6; Sucic 7 (Mario Pasalic 70, 5), Baturina 6, Vlasic 5; Matanovic 5 (Budimir 70, 5)

He belongs with Billy Wright, the first England player to 100 caps, and the man who set the England appearance record at 105 when he played for his country for the last time in 1959. He belongs with Bobby Charlton, who made it to 106 before the heartbreak of the 1970 World Cup quarter-final defeat to West Germany brought his international career to an end.

Kane belongs with Bobby Moore, Charlton's rival as the greatest England player of all time, who reached the new mark of 108 caps in November 1973. That was one of the great numbers in English sport until Peter Shilton finally surpassed it. He reached 125 caps by the time he played his last game for England in the third-place play-off at the 1990 World Cup.

It is quite some lineage. And now it is Kane who holds the prize. And if this was hardly a momentous match, it was a momentous occasion. If you are tired of glorying in a player like Kane, a relentless striker, a wonderful passer, the sweetest striker of the ball you will ever see, a player of vision, a man who exudes the beauty of simplicity and the wonder of modesty, then you are tired of football.

The honours are rushing at him in a giddy, babbling flood. It may be that he reaches close to 200 caps before he retires and even if it already seems likely that that record will be broken by Jude Bellingham, who has 61 caps at the age of 23, Kane's England goals tally, which stands at 92 after another goal against Croatia, will not be under threat for a generation or longer.

The gap, of course, is a tournament victory. That is what still separates Moore and Charlton from him. Kane is a dream of a player but he has not won the World Cup or the European Championship. What remains is the hope that he will put that right in the years that he has left in the game.

Winning the Nations League would not be quite the same but it would be a start and this victory over Croatia took England a small step closer to that goal. A convincing win over Spain in Madrid on Sunday would take them closer to their aim of finishing top of this group and getting a favourable draw in the quarter-finals in the spring.

Kane made his England debut in March 2015 when he was 21 and England's future looks brighter now than it did when he broke through. More than an hour before the game, the men who will follow Kane and perhaps even chase his caps record, chatted animatedly on the pitch. Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Gibbs-White are the new breed.

Morgan Rogers opened the scoring inside the opening half-an-hour and celebrated with his trademark cold celebration

England had found themselves pegged back by Croatia after slopping defending drew the visitors level

Referee Morten Krogh was summoned to the monitor to review the penalty shout on Thursday

Kane returned to Wembley triumphant for the first time since his historic Ballon d'Or win

After the Kane festivities, the first half was an anti-climax. Twenty-four minutes of relative drudgery ensued before Kane exhibited the breadth of his talent once again to help put England ahead. He got the ball 30 yards out, looked up and drifted a beautiful diagonal pass out to the right and into the path of Bellingham. Bellingham volleyed it across goal and Rogers forced it over the line.

The second half began slowly, too, but 15 minutes into it, Croatia equalised. England failed to clear a corner, Jarell Quansah tried to head the ball back to Jordan Pickford and, as Kane watched on, Petar Sucic stole in and hooked the ball past the England goalkeeper into the roof of the net.

Quansah made some kind of amends three minutes later when he was dragged down in the box and Danish referee Morten Krogh awarded a penalty. It was Kane-time again. Kane took the kick and lifted it gently and with a touch of curl down the centre of the goal. Dominic Livakovic dived to his left and the ball sailed softly over his trailing leg and into the net.

Croatia had chances to draw level but could not take them. England made changes and young Rio Ngumoha, a winger of rare talent, another with a rich future ahead of him, another who will help to fill the void when the day comes for Kane to bid farewell to England, came on as a late substitute for Gordon.

And so Kane's night of history began to draw to a close. In a 2-1 victory, he had made one and scored one. He remains as central to England's hopes of ending more than 60 years without a trophy as he ever has been. In a career that has festooned him with garlands and left no one in doubt of his greatness, it is the only gap that remains.

Harry Kane has set his sights firmly on rapidly reaching a century of international goals after becoming England’s most-capped player of all time.

The England skipper marked his 126th appearance for the Three Lions with the winner against Croatia in the Nations League – his first goal since picking up the Ballon d’Or last month.

Kane was afforded an emotional presentation pre-match at Wembley to mark both achievements and is already thinking of creating more history after moving within eight goals of a ton.

‘It’s achievable,’ Kane said. ‘I’m getting closer. Breaking the appearance record is a massive thing in the history of our game, seeing the tifo at the stadium and having my kids with me was beyond dreams.

‘It’s important to recognise our great players. It’s maybe something we haven’t done so well over the years with some of our other greats.

‘It's been a crazy few weeks. I don’t know if I’ve fully taken it all in. The reception has been overwhelming.

‘Maybe during the winter break I’ll be on a beach reflecting on everything I’ve achieved, having a drink with my wife.’

Croatia legend Luka Modric, 41, was part of the presentations ahead of kick off and Kane did not rule out attempting to prolong his career in a similar vein to the AC Milan midfielder.

‘He’s an inspiration for a lot of us,’ Kane added. ‘An incredible player and a great person, he’s looked after himself and still to be playing at this level is inspiring for me to push the limits. To see where your body and mentality takes you.

‘As long as I feel I can help, I’ll be here for as long as I can. If that’s until I’m 40, we’ll wait and see.’

Now qualified for the quarter-finals, England need to beat Spain in Madrid on Sunday to top their group and Thomas Tuchel believes they can topple the world champions.

‘It’s a completely different scenario, completely different setup,’ Tuchel said. ‘But I'm very positive that we will get what we want.’

#1855. Bournemouth’s Adams lauds ‘incredible manager’ Rose

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Tyler Adams lauded Marco Rose as an "incredible manager" as Bournemouth prepare to return from the international break and keep up their sparkling form.

Bournemouth went into the break on the back of a 2-1 win over Ipswich Town, which left them seventh in the Premier League.

Since a 5-1 defeat to Chelsea on October 10, the Cherries have reeled off eight straight wins across all competitions.

Only Arsenal (67), Manchester City (59), and Brighton (50) have collected more Premier League points in 2026 than Bournemouth (49 – W12 D13 L4), with the Cherries aiming to win five successive games in the top flight for the very first time when they take on Nottingham Forest on Saturday.

And though Rose had a slow start to his tenure after he replaced Andoni Iraola, Bournemouth have now hit their groove.

Rose deserves all the credit, so says Adams, who told Bournemouth's media channels: "He's an incredible manager. I'm not just saying that because he’s my manager now. The way that he looks at the game, the way that he breaks it down, I think we're going through a period of evolution, which at times takes a period of adjustment and adaptation.

"But you can see the things that we’re starting to change and the things that are starting to click at the same time.

"With the ball, we have a lot of ideas that we’re trying to execute and get guys into good positions to score goals. Some guys are playing in different positions that they weren’t accustomed to playing last year, and there's a little bit of a different formation as well. But the ideas are starting to click, and he has a lot of good ideas."

Bournemouth are competing in Europe for the first time, and Adams says the squad are learning to cope with a hectic fixture list.

He said: "It's extremely difficult. The most important thing is that you need a full squad of players, guys who are always ready to play and compete.

"When you just have Premier League games and there's one game a week, sometimes the same players play every single week. But balancing that competition, it's nearly impossible. From top to bottom, we need every single player.

"We're in a good place. The morale of the team is good. It's about finding that balance and being able to put in those Thursday, Sunday, Thursday performances over and over again, and repeat it. That's the level of consistency that we have to chase."

While Bournemouth are in fantastic form, Forest beat Manchester City before the international break to move out of the relegation zone.

#1854. Cardinale clarifies his ‘Berlusconi 2.0’ statement: “Lead the club into a new era”

Gerry Cardinale has clarified his ‘Berlusconi 2.0’ statement from about three years ago, stating that investments and resources are needed to get AC Milan back to the top.

Back in September 2023, a little over a year after he completed the purchase of Milan, Cardinale sat down with Corriere della Sera to explain his project for the club. “In football I want to be a Berlusconi 2.0, to have the same impact as him in a completely changed context,” he said, among other things.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It’s a quote that didn’t land brilliantly with some of the Milan fans, who felt that Cardinale grossly underestimated how much work Berlusconi put in with the throwaway comment. It was more than just a throwaway comment, though.

Speaking to Gazzetta dello Sport this morning, following the launch of Milan’s new holding company MSE, Cardinale clarified what he meant by the quote. It was not meant as an arrogant comparison, but rather as praise for Berlusconi and what he can learn from the legendary Milan owner.

The connection with Milan deserves a separate mention: RedBird and the city are now even more connected…

“This is the legacy we will leave in Milan. The stadium, obviously, represents a huge legacy that will transform our financial profile, but then there’s also the San Donato development project and the rest.

“If we want AC Milan to become great again, we need to close the revenue gap with the Premier League clubs. When I bought the club four years ago, I used the expression ‘Berlusconi 2.0’ and no one understood what I meant. Now perhaps we are starting to see it.”

“Everyone thought I was making an arrogant, self-centred comparison between me and Berlusconi, but that wasn’t my point. What I was trying to explain was that, just as Berlusconi transformed AC Milan and Serie A, we want to be able, through our ownership, to lead the club into a new era.

“We need to do it in the same way Berlusconi did, albeit in a modern way. I’m used to working a certain way because that’s how I do things, at the highest levels worldwide and in America.”

#1853. Sampdoria swept aside by rampant Napoli – are the Partenopei on course for their first Scudetto in 26 years?

Home » Home 2 » Sampdoria swept aside by rampant Napoli – are the Partenopei on course for their first Scudetto in 26 years?

Dries Mertens celebrating with his team-mates on the touchline after his decisive goal in the 4-2 victory at Sampdoria is typical of the spirit and togetherness that has seen Napoli storm to the top of the Serie A title. It was in dedication to Chelsea loanee Nathaniel Chabolah who recently lost his mother a a nice touch to show that there is much more to life than football, even though they have put themselves in a wonderful position to end Juventusa dominance and end a 26-year wait for the Scudetto.

Five straight wins have put Maurizio Sarria s team two points clear at the top, with the former Empoli manager breathing a new lease of life throughout a team that have always looked capable of competing for the title, yet ultimately fallen short when the pressure to deliver grew. He has transformed the entire dynamics of how Napoli play, with clinical attacking movement combined with a rock-solid defence within a 4-3-3 system that is getting the very best from the players at his disposal. This seasona s statistics proved that point; Napoli are far and away the highest scorers in Serie A this season, while only Inter Milan and Juventus have a better defensive record. Just one defeat in the twenty league games since the opening day loss at Sassuolo is another illustration of just how good Napoli have been this season, with the crushing 4-0 win at AC Milan in early October a sign of what the Partenopei are truly capable of.

Juventus were always likely to be favourites for the Scudetto on Coral and any other football odds site as their dominance of Italian football threatens to extend into its fifth season, so it is perhaps refreshing from a purista s perspective that Napoli have emerged as real contenders to challenge the Bianconeri. Massimo Allegria s side have stormed up the table in ominous fashion following a surprisingly slow start to the season, with eleven straight victories serving a serious warning to Napoli that they will make them fight all the way for the 2015/2016 Serie A title. It remains to be seen how Sarri and his team handle the pressure of having Juventus breathing down their necks, but the fact they have scored twelve goals in their last three games would indicate that

Some may have been surprised by Gonzalo Higuaina s decision to swap Real Madrid for Naples in the summer of 2013, but the 28-year-old has become one of the most feared strikers in Italy. The Argentine international has formed a wonderful strikeforce at the front of a three-man attack, with Jose Callejon and Lorenzo Insigne adding searing pace and skill on either side of a frontman who has made a career from being a true predator inside the box.

Twenty-one games in as many Serie A games this season puts him amongst the most in-form strikers in world football, with his clinical finish which opened the scoring against Sampdoria proving just how good he has been in front of goal. It is the sort of purple patch that any striker worth their salt would dream to be in; Coral have unsurprisingly backed Higuain as favourite to score in their next game against Sarria s former employers Empoli who have kept just one clean sheet from their last five league fixtures. Napoli will need Higuain to carry his rich vein of form throughout the rest of the season if they are to have any chance of maintaining their wonderful pace and sprint clear of the chasing pack.

Napoli have won many admirers across Europe for the quality of football they have played this season, but it remains to be seen if they have the mentality to pass the acid test and keep the momentum going between now and the end of the season. Recent history would suggest that their chances are not great; the Partenopei, then managed by Walter Mazzarri, put themselves in a wonderful position in 2012/2013, only to finish runners-up behind Juventus as the odd slip at the wrong times proved costly in their pursuit of Juventus. A number of third-placed finishes would also suggest that Napoli have lacked the mentality and guile to end their long wait for a Scudetto, but there is real excitement in Naples that the current crop of players have what it takes to stop the Old Lady from making it five titles in a row.

By Axel Clody | 17 Nov 2026 10:28

Arsenal have been interested in the profile of Eli Junior Kroupi for many months, and the forward should be one of the talking points of the next January transfer window. The London club have everything to be the ideal destination for the young France international.

Author of a very good 2025-26 season with Bournemouth in his first year in the Premier League, Kroupi scored 13 goals in 33 league matches. The 20-year-old striker was a revelation and quickly appeared on the radar of Europe’s biggest clubs.

‘Last summer, a fifth metatarsal injury compromised a possible departure, which the player was considering,’ - RMC Sport reported. The French outlet says the former Lorient player will be one of the attractions of the next summer transfer window, as he still interests heavyweights.

Kroupi has only just returned from his injury, however. He has played just four cameos with Bournemouth, but he reminded everyone of the extent of his talent with France. The 20-year-old won his first two caps and scored his first goal for France against Turkey (2-1).

During that international gathering, the forward made an impression and is considered one of the positives. He is highly rated by Zinedine Zidane’s staff, RMC Sport points out. His status is therefore potentially already changing, and that is before his expected transfer next summer.

While PSG, Barcelona and Bayern Munich are also interested in his profile, Arsenal have been trying to sign him for many months. Mikel Arteta is described as a fan of the new France international by TalkSport.

Viktor Gyokeres has failed to establish himself at the London club.

A departure is already being talked about for the next January transfer window. Kroupi’s profile is also compatible with Arteta’s style of play, as the Frenchman is a quick, technical striker with a great eye for goal.

Joining Arsenal would allow Kroupi to take an important step in his career by joining a top club. The English side are back among Europe’s best teams after their Premier League title win and Champions League final last year. It is one of the most attractive projects, along with that of PSG, at the moment.

However, in Paris, competition is strong at the tip of the attack with 2025 Ballon d’Or winner Ousmane Dembele, who is set to extend his contract. The problem is the same at Bayern Munich with their 2026 Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who has also signed a new deal.

In London, Kai Havertz, who can notably be repositioned behind the centre-forward, represents less and more accessible competition for Kroupi.

#1851. EPL Prepares for Most Exciting Title Race in Years

Home » Home 2 » EPL Prepares for Most Exciting Title Race in Years

Now that all of the top four English Premier League teams have had a chance to play each other, we find ourselves looking at one of the most wide open title races in recent memory. As of this writing, the league leaders are only separated by a mere six points. With the exception of Manchester City, we could very well see a new face hoisting the Premier League trophy at the end of the season.

For much of the year, it looked like Arsenal would be in the running for its first league title in more than a decade. With the Gunners’ recent victory against Leicester City, they are very much back in the conversation. Danny Welbeck returned to the pitch for the first time this season and made an immediate impact for Arsene Wenger’s squad, scoring the last-minute, game-winning goal to propel the team to within two points of the top spot. Given that even more key players are set to return to action for Arsenal in the coming months, this is easily the best shot they have had of winning a championship since their undefeated 2003-04 season.

Another surprise team that certainly deserves its own mention is Tottenham Hotspur. Following the club’s controversial defeat of Manchester City, the Spurs sit in second place, a mere two points behind Leicester City and ahead of Arsenal on goal differential. Tottenham have yet to win a title in the Premier League era and they have not won an English championship since 1961. The team has done a superb job of backing up star striker Harry Kane with a glut of promising young players, and their goal tally only helps to reinforce the wisdom behind the strategy of manager Mauricio Pochettino.

Meanwhile, Manchester City is still hoping to snag its third title as something of a swan song for exiting manager Manuel Pellegrini. It was recently announced that the club had hired Pep Guardiola . from Bayern Munich to take charge of the team beginning with next season. Thus, Pellegrini has been forced to endure the rest of the campaign as a dead man walking. Despite the impending exit of Pellegrini, City are still in the race for the Premier League title in addition to both the F.A. Cup and Champions League. Theoretically, the club could pull off a treble, if it can manage a solid string of performances during the final half of the season.

At the beginning of the season, it was expected that the usual suspects would once again dominate the league. Many predicted the reigning champs at Chelsea to repeat their success. However, a shocking season has seen the team part ways with controversial manager Jose Mourinho and struggle to remain in the top half of the tables with hopes of a Champions League spot dashed long ago.

For the first time in years, there’s a chance to see a completely new team win the league. No matter which club you support, there’s no denying that this has made for one of the most thrilling contests in recent memory. In a league where money talks, small fish like Leicester City are surprising everyone, and we can only hope that this means a new era of parity for the Premier League.

Keira Walsh is confident Chelsea are in an excellent spot after their "massive" Women's Champions League victory over Paris Saint-Germain.

Veerle Buurman turned home from Lucy Bronze's delivery in the 87th minute at Plough Lane on Wednesday.

Sjoeke Nusken had just seen an effort cleared off the line, with Buurman converting from the resulting corner.

While Chelsea had 17 shots and created chances worth 2.67 expected goals, Sonia Bompastor's team were not at their free-flowing best.

Yet they got over the line to avoid back-to-back goalless draws and, in the process, move top of the Champions League standings.

"We spoke about it before the game about wanting to finish the evening on top. We are in a good spot going into the last game."

Chelsea have kept a clean sheet in all five of their Champions League outings this season, and Walsh said: "Whoever plays in the back three, we're really solid. It's something we've concentrated on compared with last season."

The Blues have now kept six straight clean sheets in the competition, which is the longest such run by any team since Paris Saint-Germain in 2021 (six games).

Chelsea are unbeaten across their last 29 group stage/league phase games in the Champions League (W22 D7), while they have never lost a home group stage game in the competition (W13 D4).

Outgoing USA manager Mauricio Pochettino has publicly advised Pep Guardiola to pursue the vacant national team job as he prepares to begin his new role at Manchester United.

The 54-year-old Argentine will bid an emotional farewell to the Stars and Stripes when he takes charge of his final fixture against Haiti on Tuesday before officially taking over from Michael Carrick at Old Trafford.

With the US Soccer Federation now searching for a successor, former Manchester City boss Guardiola has emerged as a ‘top target’ for the vacant managerial role.

Addressing the media during his final pre-match press conference, Pochettino gave his endorsement to the legendary Catalan coach - who won 20 trophies across 10 seasons at Man City - and urged him to accept an offer if approached.

"Take it," Pochettino told reporters. "Why? Because it’s a perfect moment to arrive at the federation.

“Everything is on the right path, in the right direction. Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people – the players can fit his style."

While Pochettino is backing Guardiola for international management, a previous conversation between the pair helped trigger the Argentine's own return to the club game.

Last week, Man United confirmed Pochettino as their new head coach after dismissing Carrick, who has left the Red Devils languishing in the Premier League relegation zone following a dismal start to the campaign.

Taking the reins at Carrington marks Pochettino's first club appointment since departing Chelsea at the conclusion of the 2023-24 season, adding to previous English top-flight stints with Southampton and Tottenham Hotspur.

Pochettino was given the green light by Man United to see out his USA commitments first, with his final outing against Haiti largely a formality after the Stars and Stripes secured a dominant 6-0 win in the first leg of their CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final on Saturday.

In an interview with The Telegraph ahead of his departure, Pochettino disclosed that he confessed to Guardiola how much he longed for the daily routine of club football when the pair met at an MLS game between New York Red Bulls and New York City FC in September.

“I am ready [to return],” Pochettino explained. “This is what I miss a little bit. I miss to be, every day, with something here.

“Guardiola asked me when I was at the game, he said, ‘Oh, you don’t want to come back to the Premier League?’ I said, ‘No, I’m happy here.’

“[He said] ‘Yeah, but you don’t miss, every day, to…’ I say, ‘A little bit, yes, because you think now today, and then we have December camp against Jamaica for the MLS [players in the pool].

“But after, you need to wait [until] March. What do you do? You need to watch games, you need to travel – administrative things. That is nice, it’s good.

“But every day, to be involved: press conference, training, everything… this type of possibility, like with United, you say yes. I want that. I want to prove myself again.”

Pochettino’s candid remarks about craving a Premier League comeback may frustrate some USA supporters, given that he had put pen to paper on a new four-year contract extension just one month before his discussion with Guardiola.

#1847. Pat Cummins' remarkable 68-minute press conference took a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Usman Khawaja's integrity - Australia are in a civil war with no obvious resolution, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

Published: 05:20 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 05:21 EST, 13 November 2026

Pat Cummins is either the greatest actor in world sport – or the claim that the whole Australian team knew about the sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago is a figment of Usman Khawaja’s imagination.

After Cummins’s remarkable press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, in which he called Khawaja’s various assertions ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship, it was hard to discern any common ground, much less spot a middle way.

According to the blue corner, everyone was in on the scam, sandpaper was used not just at Cape Town but in the previous Test at Port Elizabeth, and there was a team meeting to discuss the question of collective responsibility.

According to the red, those who knew about the plan did not include the bowlers, nothing untoward happened at Port Elizabeth, and there was no meeting.

The only thing that can be said for certain after another tumultuous 24 hours for Australian cricket was that the two corners are now polar opposites, each eyeing the other with suspicion and incredulity. Barring an improbable climbdown, the twain can never meet.

Cummins, it must be said, eased into his work after an emotional start behind a lectern at the Cricket Central venue in Sydney’s Olympic Park. He began by stating his basic position, then invited questions, which for the next hour and a bit he handled with aplomb and a degree of statesmanship.

Pat Cummins held a remarkable press conference in Sydney to address the sandpaper claims

Speaking for more than an hour, Cummins dismissed Khawaja’s various assertions as ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship

This will not please those who still find it impossible to believe that Cummins and his fellow seamers on that trip, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, knew nothing of the scheme that led to bans for three batsmen – Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

After all, as any bowler will tell you, the idea that the condition of their most prized possession might be altered without their noticing is as absurd as trying to persuade a batsman to walk out without his favourite willow.

And yet. Cummins stuck to his guns, in contrast to Khawaja’s appearance on the ABC on Wednesday evening, when he repeatedly declined to name Cummins as one of the guilty party. And while Khawaja reacted to his TV grilling by cancelling media engagements, Cummins made it clear he would be answering every question that came his way.

Whichever side you believe, and whatever the doubts that remain, his press conference grabbed the momentum from Team Khawaja.

It also made the previous day’s appearance by Mitchell Marsh, Australia’s white-ball captain for the next three weeks against England, all the more bizarre. By refusing to engage with any of the questions raised by Khawaja’s autobiography, Marsh – himself a veteran of South Africa 2018 – did little to dispel the suspicion that Khawaja had a point.

And that in turn encouraged the view that Cummins, who called his own press conference without the knowledge of Cricket Australia, might be about to come clean.

Instead, he doubled down on the denial he and his bowling colleagues had issued in 2021, but now went further, taking a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Khawaja’s integrity.

‘Usman is a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,’ said Cummins. ‘He’s dealt with the way he’s presented his story in a very casual manner and it affects a lot of people. That’s what I’m grappling with at the moment, because I don’t think that’s OK. It’s not what friends do.’

Cummins plainly intended this to be his final word on the matter, but the problem facing Australian cricket is that the sore may never properly heal.

David Warner then hit back at Cummins and accused him of 'throwing Khawaja under the bus'

Only a couple of hours after Cummins finished, Warner – at Perth’s Optus Stadium as a TV pundit for the first ODI between Australia and England – was being asked for his view, and he didn’t hold back, repeating his belief that Khawaja’s version of events was ‘the truth’.

He added: ‘I really, really support him. I actually feel for him at the moment. I feel that the captain today threw Uzzy under the bus and I’m very, very disappointed about that.’

Disappointment. It’s mutual, and it’s everywhere. Cummins provided a brief distraction, but it doesn’t change the fact that this is a civil war with no obvious resolution.

Offered the chance to kick Australian cricket while it was down, England made humiliating contact with fresh air on the opening day of their eight-match white-ball trip.

Only hours after Pat Cummins had added a twist to the sandpaper saga by dismissing Usman Khawaja’s claims that the whole squad knew about the ball-tampering plans in South Africa eight years ago as ‘complete and utter nonsense’, Harry Brook’s side were blown away for 131 in the first ODI – having at one stage been 65 for eight.

Australia then romped home by seven wickets with more than 26 overs in hand to take a 1–0 lead into the second game of this three-match series in Adelaide on Sunday. For England, anyway, complete and utter nonsense felt about right.

It is not quite a year since they began their Ashes campaign here at the Optus Stadium by being bowled out in 32.5 overs in their first innings and 34.4 in their second – before stumbling to a 4–1 defeat.

Now, they obligingly split the difference, dismissed in 33.4 as Mahli Beardman, a 21-year-old fast bowler from Dunsborough, a couple of hours drive down the coast from Perth, picked up six for 34 – the best figures for Australia by an ODI debutant.

His first victim was Joe Root, caught behind for a painful 17 off 36 balls, and his second Brook, who had made only a single when he fidgeted fatally outside off stump.

That might have been enough to satisfy most newcomers, but Beardman had barely started. Jordan Cox made two before edging a poke, and Sam Curran top-edged a pull to fine leg for a duck.

When Liam Dawson, yet to score, squeezed a drive to backward point, Beardman had five wickets in 28 balls – not bad for a player whose only previous taste of international cricket had come in a T20 in Pakistan in January.

He then ended a lively last-wicket stand of 29 by removing Jofra Archer, who had just driven him down the ground for four. It was the only authentic boundary England managed off his bowling: the other, a streaky inside edge from Root, summed up the problems posed by his pace, bounce and accuracy. As bids for a place on next summer’s Ashes tour go, this was hard to ignore.

‘Laying in bed last night, that’s not what I had planned,’ said Beardman, who was taken under his wing by Australian fast-bowling legend Dennis Lillee after a mutual friend spotted him as a young teenager bowling at a bin down the side of a house. ‘It was an incredible game and it all happened so fast.’

If England had learned lessons from their collapses in the last year’s Test here, they showed little sign of being able to implement them. Players drove on the up, as they had so heedlessly a year earlier, and failed to cope with the Perth bounce.

England head coach Brendon McCullum was critical of his side's failure to adapt to the pitch, and called on them to learn from their mistakes going forward.

'It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline,' said McCullum. 'There are certain shots that are very difficult to execute. We talked about trying to put those away. We probably knew we were in for a low-scoring contest, but we expected to get a few more runs than 130.

'We're disappointed but there are some good lessons for us. If you look towards the World Cup in South Africa there’s going to be some pitches there that will test us from a bounce point of view.'

And all this after they had played a warm-up game at the WACA – a grievous omission before the Ashes – and trained with such intensity that white-ball mentor Kevin Pietersen had declared it the best practice session he had seen from an England team.

In the event, their top-scorer was Gus Atkinson, who hit an unbeaten 29 from No 10, including England’s only six.

Mitchell Marsh, stroke-less in the previous day’s press conference, put that into perspective by clearing the ropes four times during a 29-ball half-century, while Cooper Connolly – dropped by Tom Banton at midwicket on five – hit two sixes himself.

England’s only consolation had come at the start of Australia’s reply, when Atkinson bowled Travis Head first ball off the inside edge. Head it was who had taken care of Australia’s fourth-innings chase here a year ago, thrashing a 69-ball century that knocked the stuffing out of Ben Stokes’s attack.

Instead, it was Marsh who went for his shots, stopped only when he flicked Jamie Overton to Ben Duckett at deep midwicket, by which time Australia were already halfway there. For a few hours, at least, no one was talking about sandpaper.

#1846. Napoli 3-3 AC Milan Women: Lead lost twice as Rossonere claim just one point

AC Milan Women were held to a 3-3 draw in their away game against Napoli on Saturday afternoon, despite having the lead twice.

It has been a rough start to the season for Suzanne Bakker and her side, clinching a mere seven points in the first seven games. Even worse, the form seems to be declining as with today’s game included, they haven’t won in the last three games (1D, 2L).

In the derby against Inter last week, the Rossonere only had themselves to blame for the 0-3 defeat after missing several good chances, while conceding two penalties and getting a red card. They didn’t exactly make things better today either.

After just five minutes of play, the former Milan player Chante Dompig opened the scoring for the hosts. In fairness to the Rossonere, it was a cracking finish from outside the box to stun Sally Rainey in goal, so not much could be done.

Milan responded in the best way possible as Sara Kanutte Fornes pounced on a huge mistake by the Napoli defence, tapping in the equaliser after 16 minutes of play. Just ten minutes later, Abi Brighton found the striker on a corner, heading it home nicely for an early brace.

The Rossonere played well after that and headed into the break with a 2-1 lead. It wasn’t a poor start to the second half, but in the 58th minute, a really poor offside trap (of sorts) meant Napoli only had to play one pass to play Kinga Kozak through, and she made no mistakes.

Sloppy defending that Milan thought they had cancelled out in the 78th minute after a lovely move. Thea Kyvåg found Christy Grimshaw in the box with a great cross and the veteran headed it to Emma Koivisto, who in turn headed it into the back of the net.

The lead only lasted about six minutes, though, as Napoli suddenly had loads of space on the right flank and played a smart low cross into the box. Considering the lack of coverage on the flank, the Milan players at least should have kept tabs on things in the box, but they didn’t.

And so, Michela Giordano made it 3-3 and that was also the final result in the end. Two points dropped for Milan against another struggling side.
